Clinton.wildlife_intro:
Clinton's marshes and rivers put wildlife at the edge of nearly every yard. Raccoons travel the Indian and Hammonasset Rivers and work the harbor and shore neighborhoods nightly, skunks dig in the sandy shore lawns, and squirrels and bats occupy older homes from Liberty Green to Cow Hill. Muskrats live in the marsh edges, ospreys and gulls belong to the waterfront, and inland streets near the woods see woodchucks, foxes, and the occasional snake in stone walls and woodpiles.

Shore cottages are our special concern here: houses closed for winter or opened only on weekends can host a bat colony or a raccoon family for weeks before anyone notices. Additions built in stages leave roof junctions that squirrels exploit. Our crew inspects the full structure, removes the animals humanely, and seals entries so a part-time house stays secure between visits. Spring arrivals should check attics and chimneys first — it is the most common surprise our Clinton customers describe.

Cromwell.wildlife_intro:
Cromwell sits in the Connecticut River valley between Hartford and Middletown, and our crew's calls here are classic river-valley suburb work. Squirrels fill attics in the postwar and newer subdivisions, raccoons den in chimneys and raid yards backing onto the river meadows, and moles are a constant complaint in the valley soils. The Mattabesset and Connecticut Rivers bring muskrats and beavers to wet edges, bats roost in older farmhouses near the center, and skunks work the lawns at dusk across town.

Homes backing onto River Highlands' woods or the meadows see animals first and most often, because the habitat touches the yard. Our crew inspects those woods-edge homes carefully — deck voids, shed gaps, and low soffits all get used. We remove the animals humanely, seal the house, and screen the outbuildings and decks in the same plan. Fall brings the usual push of mice and squirrels indoors, and a Cromwell home sealed before the first hard frost rarely needs us in midwinter.

Essex.wildlife_intro:
Essex's three villages sit on the lower Connecticut River, and wildlife moves along the river and Falls River through all of them. Bats are our signature call in Essex Village, where captain's-era attics and chimneys have hosted summer colonies for years. Raccoons work the harbor, coves, and garbage routes in every village, squirrels use the big maples overhanging historic roofs, and skunks and woodchucks take the yards and gardens in Ivoryton and Centerbrook.

Working on Essex homes means working carefully: original trim, old masonry, and historic rooflines need sealing methods that do not damage the house, and our crew fits its work to the building. Riverfront homes also see muskrats at bulkheads and the occasional snake along stone walls and docks — usually a harmless watersnake or racer that we can identify for you. We inspect first, explain the options plainly, and time bat exclusions outside the summer pup season so colonies leave safely and do not return.

Middletown.wildlife_intro:
Middletown's wildlife work splits between its dense older core and its suburbs. Around downtown and Wesleyan, our crew handles rats in older buildings, raccoons in chimneys, pigeons on rooflines, and bats in the big historic houses on and around High Street. In Westfield, South Farms, and Newfield, the calls turn suburban: squirrels in attics, woodchucks under decks, skunks in lawns, and mice each fall. The Connecticut and Coginchaug Rivers and Wadsworth Falls' woods keep habitat woven through the city.

The older multi-family stock is where thoroughness matters most — shared walls and roofs mean an animal problem rarely belongs to one unit, and our crew inspects the building as a whole. Historic homes need careful sealing around old trim and masonry. In spring we remove denning raccoons, in summer we plan bat exclusions around the June to mid-August pause, and in fall we close up homes across the city before squirrels and rodents settle in for winter along the river.

Old Saybrook.wildlife_intro:
Old Saybrook sits where the Connecticut River meets the Sound, and the estuary drives our work here. Raccoons and skunks patrol the shore neighborhoods from Fenwick to Cornfield Point, muskrats burrow in cove banks and marsh edges, and bats summer in the attics of historic homes around Saybrook Point and Main Street. Squirrels are a steady presence in the inland neighborhoods, Canada geese gather on waterfront lawns, and ospreys over the coves are a sign of how much life the marshes support.

Shore cottages deserve a spring inspection before the season starts: a house closed since fall may have hosted squirrels, bats, or a raccoon family all winter. Homes converted from summer cottages often have layered roofs and additions where entries hide. Our crew inspects the whole house, removes animals humanely, and seals entries so the home is secure whether you are there or away. Marsh-edge properties also benefit from a look at banks and bulkheads where muskrat burrows can quietly do damage.

Portland.wildlife_intro:
Portland's brownstone history shapes its wildlife as much as its buildings. The old quarry faces and rocky ledges around town are prime snake habitat — mostly harmless racers and garter snakes, with the rocky ground being the sort of place we treat cautiously. In the neighborhoods, squirrels and bats use the quarry-era homes along Main Street, raccoons den in chimneys in Gildersleeve and the center, and woodchucks, skunks, and deer mice work the yards backing onto Meshomasic State Forest's hills.

Stone foundations and older chimneys give our Portland crew plenty of sealing to do, and homes at the forest edge see the full mix: porcupines occasionally chew outbuildings, fishers pass through, and bears are sometimes reported in the hills — animals managed by CT DEEP, though we are glad to advise on securing trash and feed. We remove the animals we are licensed for, seal houses thoroughly, and give honest guidance on the rest. Fall sealing is especially worthwhile on forest-edge streets.
